title: What lead training does OSHA require for general industry and construction?
description: OSHA lead training under 1910.1025(l) and construction 1926.62(l): action level trigger, annual refresher, topics and interim training, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) lead standards require annual training for employees exposed at or above the action level of 30 micrograms per cubic meter of air. In general industry, 29 CFR 1910.1025(l) requires training before initial job assignment and at least annually. In construction, 29 CFR 1926.62(l) requires training before job assignment and annually for anyone exposed at the action level on any day, plus interim training while exposure is still being assessed.
keyTakeaways: Both standards use the same action level, 30 micrograms per cubic meter averaged over 8 hours, and the same permissible exposure limit of 50 micrograms per cubic meter.
General industry: every employer with potential airborne lead exposure at any level must inform employees of Appendices A and B, under 1910.1025(l)(1)(i).
Construction coverage is triggered by exposure at or above the action level on any day, under 1926.62(l)(1)(ii) and (iv), which suits short duration tasks.
The construction curriculum has eight required topics, one more than general industry, including the employee's right of access to records under 29 CFR 1910.20.
OSHA opened rulemaking on both lead standards with an advance notice on June 28, 2022; as at November 2026 the training provisions in force are those described here.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: General industry employers with occupational lead exposure, such as battery manufacturing, secondary smelting, foundries and indoor firing ranges
Construction employers doing demolition, renovation, abrasive blasting, welding, cutting or torch burning where lead coatings are present, and lead abatement
Employees exposed at or above the action level, or to lead compounds that may cause skin or eye irritation

sections.heading: Which OSHA lead standard applies to which work?

blocks.text: Construction work is covered by 29 CFR 1926.62 and almost everything else by 29 CFR 1910.1025. Paragraph (a)(2) of [1910.1025](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.1025) excludes the construction industry and agricultural operations covered by part 1928. Paragraph (a) of [1926.62](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.62) picks up all construction work excluded from the general industry standard and defines it to include construction, alteration and repair, including painting and decorating, demolition, removal or encapsulation of lead materials, installation of products containing lead, and emergency cleanup.

Both standards define the action level as an airborne concentration of 30 micrograms per cubic meter of air averaged over an 8-hour period, without regard to respirator use, and set the permissible exposure limit (PEL) at 50 micrograms per cubic meter in paragraph (c). The action level is the training trigger in both.

sections.heading: What does 1910.1025(l) require in general industry?

blocks.text: General industry has two tiers. Under (l)(1)(i), every employer with "a potential exposure to airborne lead at any level" must inform employees of the content of Appendices A and B, the substance data sheet and the employee standard summary. Under (l)(1)(ii), the employer must train each employee exposed at or above the action level, or for whom skin or eye irritation is possible, and ensure participation.

Paragraph (l)(1)(iii) requires training before the time of initial job assignment for employees who become covered, and (l)(1)(iv) requires the program to be "repeated at least annually for each employee." Paragraph (l)(1)(v) lists seven topics:

items: The content of the standard and its appendices.
The specific nature of the operations that could result in exposure above the action level.
The purpose, proper selection, fitting, use and limitations of respirators.

The purpose and a description of the medical surveillance and medical removal protection programs, including adverse health effects, with particular attention to reproductive effects on both males and females.
The engineering controls and work practices associated with the employee's job assignment.
The contents of any compliance plan in effect.
Instructions that chelating agents should not routinely be used to remove lead from the body and should not be used at all except under the direction of a licensed physician.

blocks.text: Paragraph (m)(1)(iii) separately requires lead to be included in the hazard communication program and employees to be trained in accordance with the Hazard Communication Standard and paragraph (l).

sections.heading: How does construction lead training under 1926.62(l) differ?

blocks.text: The construction standard reaches more short duration work and has a longer curriculum. Paragraph (l)(1)(ii) covers each employee exposed at or above the action level "on any day", or exposed to lead compounds that may cause skin or eye irritation, naming lead arsenate and lead azide as examples. Initial training must come before job assignment under (l)(1)(iii), and (l)(1)(iv) requires the program at least annually for each employee exposed at or above the action level on any day.

Paragraph (l)(2) lists eight topics. Seven parallel the general industry list, with two differences in emphasis: the health effects topic adds hazards to the fetus and additional precautions for pregnant employees, and the controls topic adds training to follow the good work practices in Appendix B. The eighth topic is new: the employee's right of access to records under 29 CFR 1910.20. Paragraph (l)(3)(ii) also requires training materials to be provided on request to affected employees and their designated representatives, not only to OSHA.

blocks.title: Interim training before exposure is known
blocks.text: Under 1926.62(d)(2), employees doing listed tasks where lead is present, such as manual scraping or sanding of lead paint, heat gun use, abrasive blasting, welding, cutting and torch burning, must be treated as exposed above the PEL until an exposure assessment shows otherwise. The interim protection in (d)(2)(v)(F) includes hazard communication training, respirator training, and safety training under 29 CFR 1926.21, before any monitoring result exists.

sections.heading: What evidence should a lead training program produce?

blocks.text: Neither lead standard prescribes a training record in its recordkeeping paragraph, which covers exposure monitoring, medical surveillance and medical removal. Evidence of training therefore has to be designed around the triggers.

blocks.text: Respirator training under the lead standards points to the respiratory protection standard; see [OSHA respiratory protection training](/regulations/osha-respiratory-protection-training-requirements). Lead must also sit within the hazard communication program; see [OSHA hazard communication training](/regulations/osha-hazard-communication-training-requirements).

sections.heading: Are the OSHA lead standards changing?

blocks.text: OSHA has started, but not completed, a review. Its [lead rulemaking page](https://www.osha.gov/lead/rulemaking) records an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) on blood lead levels for medical removal, published June 28, 2022, with the comment period extended to October 28, 2022. OSHA states the ANPRM focuses mainly on medical removal and surveillance triggers but also seeks input on ancillary provisions including training, and that it has no impact on current enforcement. As at November 2026, the eCFR text of 1910.1025(l) and 1926.62(l) is as described on this page.

Construction employers can see how lead fits a site wide plan in [how to build a training matrix for a construction company](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix-for-a-construction-company). The overview of all OSHA training duties is at [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry keeps the general industry and construction topic lists as separate frameworks that share common concepts, so a topic such as medical removal protection is written once and assessed under each standard's wording. Exposure assessments are recorded as the events that move an employee into or out of the trained population.

faqs.q: Is OSHA lead training required every year?
faqs.a: Yes, for covered employees. Section 1910.1025(l)(1)(iv) requires the program to be repeated at least annually for each employee, and 1926.62(l)(1)(iv) requires it at least annually for each employee exposed at or above the action level on any day.

faqs.q: Does one day above the action level trigger construction lead training?
faqs.a: Yes. Paragraph 1926.62(l)(1)(ii) applies to employees exposed at or above the action level on any day. That differs from the general industry wording and captures short renovation, blasting and cutting tasks.

faqs.q: Is EPA lead renovation certification the same as OSHA lead training?
faqs.a: No. OSHA's lead standards protect workers and set the training described here. Environmental Protection Agency programs for lead-safe renovation are separate rules with their own certification, and holding one does not by itself demonstrate compliance with the topic list in 1926.62(l)(2).

faqs.q: What must workers be told about chelation?
faqs.a: Both standards require instruction that chelating agents should not routinely be used to remove lead from the body and should not be used at all except under the direction of a licensed physician. It is a required topic in 1910.1025(l)(1)(v)(G) and 1926.62(l)(2)(vii).

factCheck.claim: 1910.1025(a)(2): does not apply to construction or agricultural operations under part 1928; (b) action level 30 µg/m3 8-hour average; (c) PEL 50 µg/m3.

1910.1025(l)(1)(i)-(v): inform of Appendices A and B for potential exposure at any level; train at or above action level or irritation; before initial job assignment; at least annually; seven topics A-G.
1910.1025(l)(2)(ii) materials to Assistant Secretary and Director on request; (m)(1)(iii) lead in HCS program and training per HCS and (l).
1926.62(a) scope covers construction excluded by 1910.1025(a)(2), including painting and decorating, demolition, removal or encapsulation, installation, emergency cleanup.

1926.62(l)(1)(ii)-(iv): train at or above action level on any day or irritant compounds (lead arsenate, lead azide); before job assignment; at least annually; (l)(2)(i)-(viii) eight topics including right of access under 1910.20; (l)(3)(ii) materials to affected employees, representatives, OSHA.

1926.62(d)(2): trigger tasks (manual demolition, scraping, sanding, heat gun, abrasive blasting, welding, cutting, torch burning) treated as above PEL until assessed; (d)(2)(v)(F) interim training in HCS, respirators and 1926.21.

OSHA published ANPRM on blood lead level for medical removal June 28, 2022; comment period extended to October 28, 2022; seeks input on training among ancillary provisions; no impact on current enforcement.
